spine.skill: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 × 12
spine.rationale: Slow facts turn every ratio table, area formula, and equation into decoding work.
spine.cognitive: When fact retrieval is slow or hesitant, working memory becomes overloaded with basic computation instead of the mathematical concept. Simplifying a ratio, factoring an expression, calculating trapezoid area, or isolating a variable in 6x = 42 all collapse into laborious finger-counting or repeated addition.
spine.misconceptions: Confusing factors with multiples; serial skip-counting errors when crossing decade thresholds (e.g., 7, 14, 21, 28, 36...); viewing division as disconnected repeated subtraction rather than inverse scaling.
spine.routine: 60-Second Fact Ladder: Project 4 anchor facts (e.g., 7 × 8, 9 × 6, 12 × 4, 54 ÷ 6). Have students write answers on whiteboards and verbally explain a derivation bridge (e.g., "To get 7 × 8, I know 7 × 7 is 49, so add 7 to get 56").

spine.skill: Place a number on a scaled number line and read distance from it
spine.rationale: All of statistics and all of Unit 7; one clothesline routine rehearses both.
spine.cognitive: The scaled number line is the single most vital visual representation in middle school mathematics. It anchors statistical distributions (dot plots, box plots), connects opposites and absolute values in Unit 7, and visualizes continuous inequality solution sets in Unit 8.
spine.misconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of intervals; assuming every tick mark equals 1; misjudging fractional tick values (e.g., assuming tick between 0 and 10 is 1 rather than calculating 10 ÷ intervals); reversing negative numbers.
spine.routine: Clothesline / Number Line Flash: Draw a line with endpoints 0 and 20 partitioned into 5 equal jumps. Ask: "What is each jump worth?" Follow up: "Where does 14 live relative to the tick marks?"
spine.fallback: Grade 4 Number Lines & Lesson 7-2 (Rational Numbers on the Line).

spine.skill: Multiply and divide by 10, 100, and 1000 by shifting the decimal
spine.rationale: Makes metric conversion, percent, and benchmark estimation mental, not written.
spine.cognitive: Powers of 10 scaling transforms metric conversions, benchmark percent calculations (10%, 1%), and decimal division algorithms from tedious paper algorithms into rapid, intuitive mental shifts.
spine.misconceptions: Believing that multiplying by 10 merely means "tacking on a zero" (leading to errors like 3.4 × 10 = 3.40); shifting the decimal to the right when dividing.
spine.routine: Place-Value Shift Drill: Flash three expressions: 0.72 × 100, 4.5 ÷ 10, 0.03 × 1000. Students show answers on mini-whiteboards with arrows showing the directional decimal jump.
spine.fallback: Grade 5 Place Value Standards & Lesson 2-7 (Decimal Division).

spine.skill: Scale a pair of numbers by the same factor
spine.rationale: The whole of Unit 3 and the table work in Unit 9 are this one move, repeated.
spine.cognitive: The defining cognitive milestone of Grade 6 is moving from additive thinking to multiplicative reasoning. Ratio tables, double number lines, and bivariate linear equations all hinge on scaling both quantities by the identical constant factor.
spine.misconceptions: The Additive Trap: given 2 : 5 = 6 : __, thinking 2 + 4 = 6 so 5 + 4 = 9, rather than recognizing the multiplicative factor of 3 to produce 15.
spine.routine: Spot the Imposter Ratio: Project three candidate equivalent pairs for 4 : 7: [8 : 14], [12 : 21], [9 : 12]. Ask students which pair fell into the additive trap and why.
spine.fallback: Grade 4 Equivalent Fractions & Lesson 3-3 (Equivalent Ratios Using Tables).

spine.skill: Plot and read ordered pairs on a coordinate plane
spine.rationale: Taught with ratios, reused in Unit 7, assumed in Unit 9; a weak 3-4 costs three units.
spine.cognitive: The Cartesian coordinate plane bridges tabular numerical data and spatial geometry. Fluency in Quadrant I in Unit 3 lays the groundwork for all four quadrants in Unit 7 and bivariate linear graphs in Unit 9.
spine.misconceptions: Reversing the coordinates (moving vertically before horizontally); misreading axes that use non-unit scales (e.g., each grid line represents 2 or 5 units).
spine.routine: Run Then Jump Quick Drill: Call out an ordered pair (e.g., (5, 3) or (-4, 2)). Students state aloud the movement: "5 units across the floor, 3 units up the elevator" and point on a displayed grid.
spine.fallback: Grade 5 Quadrant I Geometry & Lesson 3-4 (Ratio Graphs).

spine.skill: Order a list of numbers least to greatest
spine.rationale: Needed for median, quartiles, IQR, and outliers. Cheap to rehearse, costly to skip.
spine.cognitive: Ordering numbers is the indispensable gatekeeper to all non-parametric statistics. A single misordered or omitted value invalidates the entire 5-number summary (median, Q1, Q3, IQR) and corrupts box plots.
spine.misconceptions: "Longer is larger" decimal fallacy (thinking 0.125 > 0.4 because 125 > 4); negative number ordering confusion (-8 is smaller than -2); dropping duplicate values in a list.
spine.routine: 5-Card Rapid Sort: Post five unsorted numbers on the board (e.g., 0.4, 0.25, 0.08, 0.5, 0.19). Students write them in order in 30 seconds and circle the median.
spine.fallback: Grade 4 Whole Number Comparison & Grade 5 Decimal Comparison (Lesson 2-3).

spine.skill: Move among a fraction, a decimal, and a percent
spine.rationale: All of Unit 4, plus placing rational numbers in Unit 7.
spine.cognitive: Fractions, decimals, and percents are not three separate concepts; they are interchangeable dialects of rational numbers. Fluency with benchmarks (1/4=0.25=25%, 1/10=0.10=10%, 1/2=0.50=50%) anchors mental estimation.
spine.misconceptions: Treating decimals and percents as numerically identical (e.g., equating 0.4 with 4% instead of 40%); not simplifying fractions over 100.
spine.routine: Benchmark Triplet Call-and-Response: Teacher states: "Three-fourths!" Students write: 0.75 and 75%. Teacher states: 0.05; students respond: 5% and 1/20.

spine.skill: Follow order of operations, including parentheses and exponents
spine.rationale: Every formula and evaluation depends on it; trapezoid area is where it first bites.
spine.cognitive: Hierarchical operations (PEMDAS / GEMDAS) govern all mathematical evaluation. Geometry formulas (trapezoids: 1/2(b1+b2)h) and algebraic expressions fail immediately if computed left-to-right.
spine.misconceptions: Performing addition before multiplication (e.g., 4 + 3 × 2 = 14 instead of 10); treating exponents as multiplication (evaluating 2³ as 6 instead of 8); ignoring parentheses.
spine.routine: Circle the First Move: Project 3 + 4 × 2² − (5 + 1). Ask students: "Do not calculate the answer. State only which operation is performed first, and which is performed second."
spine.fallback: Grade 5 Numerical Expressions & Lesson 6-4 (Order of Operations with Powers).

spine.skill: Name the inverse of an operation and check by substituting back
spine.rationale: The solving move in Unit 8, and the self-check that makes an answer trustworthy.
spine.cognitive: The balance concept of algebraic equations relies entirely on operational inverses. Substitution provides the essential mathematical self-check that transforms students from passive answer-getters into self-correcting thinkers.
spine.misconceptions: Viewing the equals sign as an operation prompt ("calculate now") rather than a balance relation; repeating the original operation instead of choosing its inverse, or applying an operation to only one side.
spine.routine: Undo & Prove: Display m + 14 = 30. Ask: 1) What operation undoes +14? 2) What is m? 3) Substitute your answer to prove the equation balances.

spine.skill: Add a list of numbers to a running total
spine.rationale: Means, MAD, surface area, and perimeter all end in one careful sum.
spine.cognitive: Complex statistical measures (mean, MAD) and geometric calculations (perimeter, multi-face prism surface area) end in a multi-addend sum. A single computational error ruins otherwise flawless conceptual work.
spine.misconceptions: Losing track when summing 6+ numbers; misaligning decimal places; failure to group compatible numbers (making tens/hundreds).
spine.routine: Make-a-Ten Combinations: Project a string of 6 numbers: 12, 18, 25, 15, 9, 11. Have students bracket compatible pairs (12+18=30, 25+15=40, 9+11=20) to compute 90 mentally.
spine.fallback: Grade 4 Addition Algorithm & Lesson 2-8 (Finding the Mean).

spine.skill: Find the area of a rectangle and of a triangle
spine.rationale: Every other figure in Unit 5 is decomposed into these two.
spine.cognitive: Rectangles and triangles are the foundational atoms of 2D and 3D geometry. Every polygon (parallelogram, trapezoid, rhombus, composite) and every 3D net in Grade 6 decomposes into these two shapes.
spine.misconceptions: Using the slanted edge instead of the true perpendicular height; forgetting the 1/2 factor in triangle area; confusing area (coverage) with perimeter (boundary).
spine.routine: Perpendicular Detective: Display a non-right triangle and a slanted parallelogram with 3 labeled side lengths. Students identify which dimension is the genuine perpendicular height.

spine.skill: Multiply and divide with fractions and mixed numbers
spine.rationale: Carried from Grade 5 and never retired; it returns in area, volume, and equations.
spine.cognitive: Fraction and mixed number multiplication/division is carried from Grade 5 and applied constantly across Grade 6 in fractional volume, polygon area, and rational algebraic coefficients.
spine.misconceptions: Multiplying mixed numbers without converting to improper fractions (e.g., 2 1/2 × 3 1/2 ≠ 6 1/4); inverting the dividend instead of the divisor when dividing fractions.
spine.routine: Improper & Reciprocal Sprint: Flash 2 3/4. Students write improper fraction (11/4) and reciprocal (4/11) on whiteboards in under 20 seconds.

units.title: Statistics and Data Displays
units.premise: Order a list of numbers, read a scaled number line, and add then divide a set of values. A student who cannot order numbers cannot find a median, a quartile, or an outlier.

lessons.title: Understand Statistical Questions
lessons.subtopics: Statistical Questions · Dot Plots and Shape

skills.text: Order a list of up to 10 whole numbers least to greatest
Read a scaled number line and say what one tick mark is worth
Tally and count a set of up to 30 responses without losing place
Compare two whole numbers and say which is greater

lessons.quick_check: Order 7, 3, 12, 5, 9. On a line from 0 to 10 split into 5 equal jumps, what is one jump worth?
lessons.solution:
Ordered list: 3, 5, 7, 9, 12.
Line jump value: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 units per jump.
lessons.diagnostic: If students say 1 jump = 1, they are reflexively counting tick marks rather than dividing the total distance (10) by the number of intervals (5). Dot plots require understanding scale increments.

spine_links.skill: Place a number on a scaled number line and read distance from it
Order a list of numbers least to greatest

lessons.title: Represent and Describe Data in a Histogram
lessons.subtopics: Building a Histogram · Describing Histogram Shape

skills.text: Decide which interval a value belongs to (is 19 in 10–19 or 20–29?)
Sort up to 20 values into given intervals and count each bin
Add a column of one- and two-digit numbers to a total
Read a graph scale that skip-counts by 2, 5, or 10

lessons.quick_check: Which interval holds 29: 20–29 or 30–39? How many of 4, 11, 19, 21, 25 land in 10–19?
lessons.solution:
Interval assignment: 29 belongs in the 20–29 interval.
Bin count: Values in 10–19 are 11 and 19 (Total = 2 values).
lessons.diagnostic: If students place 29 in 30–39, they confuse boundary conventions. For these whole-number bins, include both stated endpoints. Histogram bins must not overlap; specify which bin contains each boundary value. Clarify the boundary before building frequency tables.

spine_links.skill: Add a list of numbers to a running total

lessons.title: Describe the Data Using the Median
lessons.subtopics: Finding the Median · Median of an Even Set

skills.text: Order up to 12 numbers least to greatest
Find the middle position of an odd-length list by counting in from both ends
Find the number halfway between two numbers
Divide a two-digit sum by 2

lessons.quick_check: Put in order: 9, 4, 15, 6, 11. What number is halfway between 12 and 17?
lessons.solution:
Ordered list: 4, 6, 9, 11, 15 (Middle value = 9).
Halfway point: (12 + 17) ÷ 2 = 29 ÷ 2 = 14.5 (or 14 1/2).
lessons.diagnostic: Finding the midpoint between two numbers with an odd difference requires decimal division or mixed numbers. If students answer 14 or 15, they will struggle with the median of even-sized data sets.
lessons.reteach: Grade 5 Division with Decimals & Midpoint Routines

spine_links.skill: Place a number on a scaled number line and read distance from it
Order a list of numbers least to greatest

lessons.title: Represent and Describe Data in a Box Plot
lessons.subtopics: Building a Box Plot · Comparing Box Plots

skills.text: Order a data set and find its median
Split an ordered list into a lower half and an upper half
Subtract two-digit whole numbers
Plot a point at the right place on a scaled number line

lessons.quick_check: Ordered: 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 14, 18, 20. Find the median of the lower half.
lessons.solution:
Ordered list split: [3, 5, 8, 10] | [12, 14, 18, 20].
Lower half: 3, 5, 8, 10.
Median of lower half (Q1): (5 + 8) ÷ 2 = 13 ÷ 2 = 6.5.
lessons.diagnostic: Box plots require partitioning the ordered set into equal lower and upper halves. If students include the overall median in the lower half or fail to average 5 and 8, review Lesson 2-3.

spine_links.skill: Place a number on a scaled number line and read distance from it
Order a list of numbers least to greatest

lessons.title: Describe Data by Range and Interquartile Range
lessons.subtopics: Range and IQR · Comparing Variability

skills.text: Find the maximum and minimum of a data set
Subtract whole numbers, including across zeros
Locate Q1 and Q3 in an ordered set
Compare two differences to say which spread is larger

lessons.quick_check: Range of 12, 7, 19, 4, 15? If Q1 = 6 and Q3 = 17, what is Q3 − Q1?
lessons.solution:
Range: Maximum − Minimum = 19 − 4 = 15.
IQR: Q3 − Q1 = 17 − 6 = 11.
lessons.diagnostic: If students subtract 12 − 7, they took the first two numbers in the raw list rather than identifying max and min. Emphasize that spread measures require finding extreme order values.
lessons.reteach: Grade 4 Subtraction Across Place Values & Lesson 2-4

spine_links.skill: Place a number on a scaled number line and read distance from it
Order a list of numbers least to greatest

lessons.title: Divide Multi-Digit Numbers Using an Algorithm
lessons.subtopics: Estimate Quotients · Whole-Number Division · Interpret Remainders

skills.text: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 × 12
Use place value to divide hundreds, tens, and ones
Subtract multi-digit whole numbers with regrouping
Estimate a quotient and check with multiplication

lessons.quick_check: Compute 156 ÷ 6. Explain how multiplication checks your quotient.
lessons.solution:
156 ÷ 6 = 26.
Divide 15 tens by 6: 2 tens with 3 tens remaining. Combine those 3 tens with 6 ones to get 36 ones. Divide 36 by 6 to get 6 ones.
Check: 26 × 6 = 156.
lessons.diagnostic: Watch for a quotient of 21 with a remainder of 30. A remainder must be less than the divisor; rename the remaining tens as ones before continuing.
lessons.reteach: Grade 4 place-value division and the relationship between multiplication and division

spine_links.skill: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 × 12
Name the inverse of an operation and check by substituting back

lessons.title: Divide Decimals Using an Algorithm
lessons.subtopics: Dividing a Decimal by a Whole Number · Dividing by a Decimal

skills.text: Recall division facts through 12 × 12
Divide multi-digit whole numbers with the standard algorithm
Multiply and divide by 10, 100, 1000 by shifting the decimal point
Line up decimal places and annex zeros to keep dividing

lessons.solution:
84 ÷ 4 = 21
4.8 ÷ 2 = 2.4
0.6 × 100 = 60 (shift decimal 2 places right and annex zero).
lessons.diagnostic: If students write 0.6 × 100 = 6 or 6.0, they only shifted one place. Shifting and annexing zeros is critical for the standard decimal division algorithm.
lessons.reteach: Grade 5 Decimal Operations & Place Value Shifts

spine_links.skill: Multiply and divide by 10, 100, and 1000 by shifting the decimal

lessons.title: Describe Data Using the Mean
lessons.subtopics: Finding the Mean · Reaching a Target Mean

skills.text: Add a list of 5–10 two-digit numbers accurately
Divide a three-digit number by a one-digit number
Count how many values are in a data set
Find a missing addend that reaches a given total

lessons.quick_check: Mean of 10, 14, 8, 12, 16? What must be added to 48 to reach 60?
lessons.solution:
Sum: 10 + 14 + 8 + 12 + 16 = 60.
Count: 5 values.
Mean: 60 ÷ 5 = 12.
Missing addend: 60 − 48 = 12.
lessons.diagnostic: The mean requires two distinct operations: multi-addend summation followed by division. A failure in either step collapses the calculation. Rehearsing running totals is essential.
lessons.reteach: Grade 4 Multi-digit Addition & Grade 5 Long Division

spine_links.skill: Add a list of numbers to a running total

lessons.title: Describe Data by Mean Absolute Deviation
lessons.subtopics: Finding the MAD · Comparing Sets with MAD

skills.text: Find the mean of a data set
Subtract to find the distance between two numbers and keep it positive
Add a list of distances
Divide a total by the number of values

lessons.quick_check: The mean is 20. How far is 26 from the mean? How far is 14?
lessons.solution:
Distance of 26: |26 − 20| = 6.
Distance of 14: |14 − 20| = 6.
(Both distances are strictly 6 units).
lessons.diagnostic: Students who answer −6 for 14 have not internalized that distance is nonnegative and equals zero when a value equals the mean. This misconception will corrupt Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD), which averages absolute distances.

spine_links.skill: Add a list of numbers to a running total

lessons.title: Choose Appropriate Measures
lessons.subtopics: Mean or Median? · Matching Center and Spread

skills.text: Compute mean, median, range, IQR, and MAD on demand
Spot an outlier in a short list
Read a dot plot or histogram as symmetric or skewed
Compare two measures and say which is pulled by an extreme value

lessons.quick_check: Which measure of center fits 2, 3, 3, 4, 50 — mean or median? Why?
lessons.solution:
Best Measure: Median (3).
Why: 50 is an extreme outlier that skews the data. The mean is 62 ÷ 5 = 12.4, which is higher than 4 out of the 5 data values and does not represent the center. The median (3) accurately reflects the typical value.
lessons.diagnostic: Tests student ability to choose between mean and median based on shape and skewness. If students choose mean, review how extreme values pull the balance point.

units.title: Ratios and Rates
units.premise: Multiplication and division facts, and scaling a pair of numbers by the same factor. Every ratio table, graph, comparison, and conversion in this unit is that one move repeated.

lessons.title: Understand Ratios
lessons.subtopics: Understand Ratios · Ratios with Tape Diagrams

skills.text: Recall multiplication facts through 12 × 12
Skip-count by any one-digit number
Count each part of a part-whole picture, then add the parts for the total
Write a fraction naming a part of a whole

lessons.quick_check: 6 × 4? There are 3 dogs and 5 cats — how many animals in all?
lessons.solution:
6 × 4 = 24.
Total animals: 3 dogs + 5 cats = 8 animals total.
(Part-to-part ratio is 3 : 5; part-to-whole ratio of dogs is 3 : 8).
lessons.diagnostic: Ratios require distinguishing part-to-part from part-to-whole relationships. Students must sum the parts to establish the whole before writing part-to-whole fractions.
lessons.reteach: Grade 3 Multiplication Facts & Grade 4 Part-Whole Fractions

spine_links.skill: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 × 12

lessons.title: Rates and Unit Rates
lessons.subtopics: Understanding Unit Rates · Comparing Unit Prices (Best Buy)

skills.text: Divide a multi-digit number by a one- or two-digit number
Divide to find the amount for one, and read “per” as “for each one”
Keep a repeating pattern going in a table
Attach the correct unit label to a computed number

lessons.quick_check: 60 ÷ 4? If 4 pencils cost $2, what does 1 pencil cost?
lessons.solution:
60 ÷ 4 = 15.
Unit price: 1 pencil costs $2.00 ÷ 4 = $0.50 (50 cents).
lessons.diagnostic: Unit price requires dividing cost by quantity ($2 ÷ 4). Students who instinctively divide larger by smaller (4 ÷ 2 = $2) make the #1 error in rate reasoning.

spine_links.skill: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 × 12

lessons.title: Equivalent Ratios Using Tables
lessons.subtopics: Modeling Clay Recipe (ratio tables) · The Bridge Strategy (Scaling Ratios)

skills.text: Multiply both numbers of a pair by the same factor
Recall multiplication facts through 12 × 12
Write equivalent fractions by multiplying numerator and denominator
Fill the next row of a growing pattern table

lessons.solution:
2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 5 = 15.
Complete ratio: Since 2 × 4 = 8, scale 3 by 4: 3 × 4 = 12 (2 : 3 = 8 : 12).
lessons.diagnostic: The additive trap: students who add 6 to 3 to get 9 fail to see multiplicative scaling. Emphasize multiplying both quantities by the identical scale factor.

spine_links.skill: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 × 12
Scale a pair of numbers by the same factor

lessons.title: Equivalent Ratios Using Graphs
lessons.subtopics: Graphing Ratios on Coordinate Planes · Interpreting Points on Ratio Graphs

skills.text: Plot a point in Quadrant I from an ordered pair
Read the scale on each axis before plotting
Count right from the origin, then up
Build a ratio table to generate the pairs

lessons.quick_check: Start at (0, 0), move 3 units right and 2 units up — write the ordered pair. A horizontal axis has grid lines every 5 units, starting at 0. How many intervals right of 0 is the value 15?
lessons.solution:
Ordered pair: (3, 2) — move 3 units right on x-axis, then 2 units up on y-axis.
Grid position: If each grid line is 5, 15 is at line 3 (15 ÷ 5 = 3).
lessons.diagnostic: Watch for coordinate inversion: writing (2, 3) instead of (3, 2). Also verify that students divide by the grid step size when axes do not count by 1.

spine_links.skill: Scale a pair of numbers by the same factor
Plot and read ordered pairs on a coordinate plane

lessons.title: Comparing Ratio Relationships
lessons.subtopics: Comparing Ratios with Common Terms · Comparing Rates with Benchmarks

skills.text: Compare two whole numbers
Scale both parts of a ratio to hit a target value
Find a common multiple of two numbers
Divide to find a unit rate for a fair comparison

lessons.quick_check: Which is greater, 12 or 9? Scale 3 : 4 so the first number is 12.
lessons.solution:
12 is greater than 9.
Scale 3 : 4: Since 3 × 4 = 12, multiply 4 by 4 to get 16. Scaled ratio: 12 : 16.
lessons.diagnostic: Comparing ratios requires scaling to a common term (like finding common denominators). If students scale only the first term, ratio equivalence is broken.

spine_links.skill: Scale a pair of numbers by the same factor

skills.text: Recall multiplication and division facts

Multiply and divide by 10, 100, 1000 for metric steps
Decide whether a conversion calls for multiplying or dividing

lessons.quick_check: 12 × 4? 1 foot = ___ inches? 2.5 m = ___ cm?
lessons.diagnostic: Students must know whether to multiply or divide based on unit size: converting large units to small units requires multiplying by the conversion factor.

lessons.title: Converting Between Systems
lessons.subtopics: Customary vs. Metric Conversions · Multi-Step System Conversions and Dosage

skills.text: Multiply a whole number by a decimal
Round a decimal to the nearest tenth or hundredth
Multiply by a conversion factor and keep the unit label
Chain two conversions in order without losing a step

lessons.quick_check: 4 × 1.6? 10 × 0.45? Round 6.44 to the nearest tenth.
lessons.solution:
4 × 1.6 = 6.4.
10 × 0.45 = 4.5.
Round 6.44 to nearest tenth = 6.4 (since the hundredths digit 4 is less than 5).
lessons.diagnostic: Cross-system conversions produce decimals that require rounding. Students must multiply decimals accurately and apply correct rounding rules.

lessons.title: Understand Percent
lessons.subtopics: Percent Means Per Hundred · Percents Greater Than 100%

skills.text: Read and write a fraction with denominator 100
Count shaded squares on a 100-square grid
Write hundredths as a decimal
Simplify a fraction over 100

lessons.quick_check: 37 of 100 squares are shaded — write it as a fraction, a decimal, and a percent.
lessons.solution:
Fraction: 37/100.
Decimal: 0.37.
Percent: 37%.
lessons.diagnostic: Percent literally means 'per hundred'. If students write 3.7% or 0.037, review base-10 hundredths grid models before proceeding.
lessons.reteach: Grade 4/5 Fractions and Decimals with Denominator 100

lessons.title: Relate Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages
lessons.subtopics: Fractions, Decimals, Percents · Compare and Order

skills.text: Multiply and divide by 100 by shifting the decimal point
Write a fraction as a decimal by dividing
Recall benchmark equivalents for 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 3/4, 1/10
Compare decimals to the hundredths place

lessons.quick_check: 0.45 as a percent? 25% as a fraction in simplest form? Which is greater, 0.6 or 55%?
lessons.solution:
0.45 = 45%.
25% in simplest form: 25/100 = 1/4.
Comparison: 0.6 = 60%, so 0.6 is greater than 55%.
lessons.diagnostic: Students who say 55% is greater than 0.6 mistakenly compare 55 to 6. Converting all values to percents (60% vs 55%) or decimals (0.60 vs 0.55) makes the relationship obvious.

Order a list of numbers least to greatest

lessons.title: Estimate the Percent of a Number
lessons.subtopics: Estimate with Benchmarks · Estimate a Percent of a Number

skills.text: Find 10% of a number by shifting the decimal one place left
Find 1% of a number by shifting two places left
Halve and double a number mentally
Round to a compatible number that is easy to take a percent of

lessons.solution:
10% of 320 = 32 (shift decimal 1 place left).
1% of 320 = 3.2 (shift decimal 2 places left).
Half of 32 = 16 (which represents 5% of 320).
lessons.diagnostic: Benchmark percents (10%, 1%, 50%) build mental estimation. If students attempt long multiplication (0.10 × 320), rehearse decimal shifting shortcuts.
lessons.reteach: Grade 5 Powers of 10 & Mental Math Halving

lessons.title: Find and Compare with Percentages
lessons.subtopics: Find the Percent of a Number · Compare with Percents

skills.text: Write a percent as a decimal
Multiply a whole number by a decimal
Multiply a whole number by a fraction
Compare two products to decide which is larger

lessons.quick_check: 0.25 × 80? 3/4 of 80? Which is more: 20% of 50 or 30% of 40?
lessons.solution:
0.25 × 80 = 20.
3/4 of 80 = 60.
Comparison: 20% of 50 = 10; 30% of 40 = 12.
30% of 40 is more (12 > 10).
lessons.diagnostic: Finding percent of a number requires converting percent to a decimal or fraction and multiplying. Check whether students recognize 0.25 as 1/4.
lessons.reteach: Lesson 4-2 (Relate Fractions, Decimals, Percents) & Grade 5 Multiplication

Multiply and divide with fractions and mixed numbers

lessons.title: Determine the Whole Given the Part and Percent
lessons.subtopics: Find the Whole · Solve for the Whole

skills.text: Divide a whole number by a decimal
Tell which number is the part and which is the whole
Divide by a benchmark fraction such as 1/4 or 1/2
Check an answer by multiplying back

lessons.quick_check: 12 ÷ 0.25? 12 is 25% of what number? Now check: 25% of your answer.
lessons.solution:
12 ÷ 0.25 = 48.
The whole is 48 (12 is 25% of 48).
Check: 25% of 48 = 0.25 × 48 = 12 (balances!).
lessons.diagnostic: Solving for the whole reverses the percent equation: Whole = Part ÷ Percent. If students multiply 12 × 0.25 = 3, they found 25% of 12 instead of the whole.

lessons.quick_check: Area of an 8 cm by 5 cm rectangle? In a parallelogram, is the height the slanted side?
lessons.solution:
Rectangle area = 8 cm × 5 cm = 40 cm².
Height question: No! The height must be perpendicular to the base, never the slanted side.

lessons.solution:
7 × 4 = 28, then half = 14.
Triangle area: A = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 7 m × 4 m = 14 m².

lessons.solution:
Parentheses first: (6 + 10) = 16.
Area = 1/2 × 16 × 4 = 8 × 4 = 32 square units.
lessons.diagnostic: Trapezoid formula: A = 1/2(b1 + b2)h requires executing order of operations inside parentheses before scaling. Check that students sum the parallel bases first.

Large rectangle area: 10 × 6 = 60.
Cutout rectangle area: 3 × 2 = 6.
Area remaining: 60 − 6 = 54 square units.

lessons.solution:
A rectangular prism has 6 faces.
That forms 3 matching pairs of congruent opposite faces (top/bottom, front/back, left/right).

lessons.solution: Surface Area = 12 + 12 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 = 24 + 40 + 30 = 94 square units.

lessons.quick_check: 4.8 ÷ 2? How many fourths are in 3? Reciprocal of 5?
lessons.solution:
4.8 ÷ 2 = 2.4.
There are 12 fourths in 3 (since 3 ÷ 1/4 = 3 × 4 = 12).
Reciprocal of 5 is 1/5.
lessons.diagnostic: Dividing by a fraction means finding how many of that fraction fit into the whole. Students must connect dividing by 1/4 to multiplying by 4.

lessons.solution:
2 3/4 as improper fraction: (2 × 4 + 3) / 4 = 11/4.
Reciprocal of 3/5 is 5/3.
Product: 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.
lessons.diagnostic: Fraction division requires inverting the divisor and multiplying. Students must convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before applying reciprocals.

lessons.quick_check: 4 + 6 ÷ 2? 3 + 2² × 5? Which operation comes first?
lessons.solution:
4 + 6 ÷ 2: Divide first (6 ÷ 2 = 3), then add: 4 + 3 = 7.
3 + 2² × 5: Exponent first (2² = 4), then multiply (4 × 5 = 20), then add: 3 + 20 = 23.
Exponent comes first, then multiplication, then addition.
lessons.diagnostic: Students who compute left-to-right get (4+6)÷2 = 5 and (3+4)×5 = 35. Rigorous order of operations practice is needed.

lessons.quick_check: Evaluate 4n + 3 when n = 5. Write an expression for “7 more than a number.”
lessons.solution:
When n = 5: 4(5) + 3 = 20 + 3 = 23.
Expression for '7 more than a number': n + 7 (or x + 7).
lessons.diagnostic: Substituted variable: ensure students recognize that 4n means 4 times n, not the digits '45'. Check algebraic syntax translations.

lessons.subtopics: Simplifying to Show Equivalence · Testing Equivalence by Substituting

Evaluate an expression at a chosen value

lessons.quick_check: 5x + 2x = ? Evaluate 2(x + 3) and 2x + 6 at x = 4 — are they the same?
lessons.solution:
5x + 2x = 7x.
At x = 4: 2(4 + 3) = 2(7) = 14; and 2(4) + 6 = 8 + 6 = 14.
Yes, both equal 14 at x = 4. The distributive property, 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6, shows they are equivalent for every x.
lessons.diagnostic: Combining like terms requires adding coefficients while keeping the variable identical. Matching at one input checks that case; use properties of operations to establish equivalence for every input.

lessons.quick_check: All the factors of 18? First five multiples of 6? GCF of 18 and 24?
lessons.solution:
Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
First five multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30.
GCF of 18 and 24: Common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6; Greatest is 6.
lessons.diagnostic: Students constantly confuse factors (numbers that divide into 18) with multiples (numbers 18 divides into). Clarify definitions before factoring polynomials.

lessons.solution:
Opposite of −6 is +6 (or 6).
Position of −3: sits 3 units to the left of 0 (or 3 units below 0).

lessons.solution:
2.7 falls between integers 2 and 3.
−11/2 = −5.5, which falls between −6 and −5 (exactly halfway between them).

lessons.solution:
|−9| = 9.
Distance from −4 to 0 is 4 units.
Distance from −4 to 3: 4 units (to zero) + 3 units (to 3) = 7 units total.

lessons.solution:
−6 < −2 (since −6 is further to the left on the number line).
Ordered least to greatest: −3, −1/2, 0, 1.5.
lessons.diagnostic: The negative magnitude fallacy: students think −6 > −2 because 6 > 2. Ground ordering on the number line: left is always less, right is always greater.

Substitute x = 4: 3(4) = 12 is true, so YES, x = 4 is a solution.

lessons.solution:
m − 11 = 25 → m = 25 + 11 = 36.

x ÷ 5 = 9 → x = 9 × 5 = 45.
